hints: Focus on what must happen at the same time, a gas bubbling off plus a new white solid forming that is different from the starting solid.
Remember that Group 2 metals with dilute acids give hydrogen gas, while Group 2 carbonates with acids give carbon dioxide gas.
Now check solubility, magnesium sulfate is very soluble but calcium sulfate is sparingly soluble and forms a white precipitate, so link the gas to the new solid.
walkthrough:
**List what we must observe**

We need two products at once. A colourless gas must bubble off, and a new white precipitate must appear that is not the original solid T.

So T must react completely with excess U.

**Check the gas each pair could make**

Metals + dilute acid give hydrogen, carbonates + acid give carbon dioxide.

$$\text{M(s) + H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{MSO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{(g)}$$ 
$$\text{MCO}_3\text{(s) + 2H}^+\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{M}^{2+}\text{(aq) + CO}_2\text{(g) + H}_2\text{O(l)}$$

**Check the precipitate using solubility**

For a new white precipitate we need an insoluble or sparingly soluble product. $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble, $\text{SrCl}_2$ is soluble, so no precipitate there. $\text{CaSO}_4$ is sparingly soluble and appears as a white precipitate.

$$\text{Ca(s) + H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{CaSO}_4\text{(s) + H}_2\text{(g)}$$

**Confirm the match**

Here T, calcium metal, is used up, the gas is colourless $\text{H}_2$, and the white solid is new $\text{CaSO}_4$, not T. This fits all three conditions perfectly.

options.A: Barium carbonate is insoluble in water and does not react with water alone. No gas is evolved and no new precipitate forms, any white solid seen would just be unreacted T.
options.B: Calcium reacts vigorously with dilute sulfuric acid to give colourless hydrogen gas and sparingly soluble white calcium sulfate. The calcium is used up, so the precipitate is a new product, not T.
options.C: Magnesium does react with dilute sulfuric acid to give colourless hydrogen gas, but the product magnesium sulfate, $\text{MgSO}_4$, is very soluble. No white precipitate would be seen.
options.D: Strontium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give colourless carbon dioxide gas, but the product strontium chloride, $\text{SrCl}_2$, is soluble. No white precipitate forms in excess acid.
